chapters.title: Chapter 2: Global Cycles That Shaped Modern Markets

lessons.title: Tulips, the South Sea, and Railway Mania: The First Speculative Cycles

body.text: The assets change: flower bulbs, trading monopolies, railway lines, dot-com stocks, SME IPOs. The script barely changes at all. A real new opportunity, easy credit, a crowd that stops asking about price, and a collapse that surprises almost everyone who was inside it.

children.text: Chapter 1 gave you the toolkit: cycles, overlapping engines, and credit as the fuel. This chapter applies it to history. We start with three episodes from the 1600s to the 1800s that are still quoted in almost every discussion of bubbles. Each one teaches something different. Tulips show how quickly a story can outrun reality. The South Sea Company shows what happens when the seller of shares also lends you the money to buy them. Railway Mania shows that a technology can transform the world and still ruin the people who invested in it at the wrong price.
Tulip Mania: Holland, 1636 to 1637

markDefs.definition: An agreement to buy or sell something at a fixed price on a future date. The buyer does not pay the full price today, which makes it a form of leverage.

children.text: In the early 1600s the Dutch Republic was the richest trading nation in Europe, and tulips, recently arrived from the Ottoman Empire, became a status symbol. Rare varieties with streaked, flame-like petals were especially prized. The streaks were actually caused by a virus, so nobody could reliably breed them, which made them scarce. Through the winter of 1636 to 1637, while the bulbs were still in the ground, traders in taverns began buying and selling promises to deliver bulbs in spring. These were effectively
forward contracts

, and very little cash changed hands. Prices for some bulbs multiplied within weeks. In early February 1637, at a routine bulb auction in Haarlem, buyers simply failed to show up. Within days the market froze, and prices collapsed.

body.label: The price of a status symbol
body.value: Several thousand guilders for a single rare bulb
body.context: Contemporary accounts record the rarest bulbs changing hands for thousands of guilders at the peak, at a time when a skilled craftsman earned very roughly 300 guilders a year. These figures come from a small number of sources and should be treated as illustrative.

body.text: Much of the popular tulip story comes from Charles Mackay's 1841 book Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds, written two centuries after the event. Modern historians, notably Anne Goldgar in her 2007 study, found that the mania involved a fairly small group of merchants and artisans, that many contracts were settled for a small fraction of the agreed price or never enforced, and that the Dutch economy was not ruined. Keep both lessons: prices really did detach from any sensible value, and dramatic crash stories get exaggerated with each retelling.

children.text: The South Sea Bubble: London, 1720

The South Sea Company was set up in 1711 and given a monopoly on British trade with Spain's colonies in South America, a trade that in practice turned out to be small and heavily restricted. Its real business became government finance. In 1720 it won the right to take over a large part of Britain's national debt: holders of government bonds could swap them for South Sea shares. The higher the share price, the fewer shares the company needed to issue for each bond, and the more profit it kept. The company therefore had every incentive to push its share price up, and it did.

stats.label: Peak, summer 1720
stats.context: Roughly seven times higher in about six months

stats.label: End of 1720
stats.context: A fall of more than 80% from the peak

body.title: How the South Sea Company fed its own bubble

children.text: Pay later:
new shares were sold on instalments, with only a small part of the price due upfront, so buyers could control far more shares than they could afford.
Loans against its own shares:
the company lent money to investors using South Sea shares as collateral, so it was financing the demand for its own stock. This is the credit loop from Lesson 1.3 in its purest form.
Friends in high places:
shares were given or sold on favourable terms to politicians and courtiers, which bought political support and lent the scheme credibility.
Crushing the competition:

the Bubble Act of June 1720 banned joint-stock companies operating without a royal charter. It was backed by the South Sea Company, partly to stop rival share schemes from drawing money away from its own stock.

Once the price stalled in the late summer of 1720, the machine ran in reverse. Instalments fell due, loans secured on shares were no longer safe, and insiders who understood the scheme sold. Thousands of investors were ruined, including many from the gentry and the professions. Isaac Newton is often said to have lost heavily after buying back in near the top, though the exact size of his loss is uncertain. A parliamentary inquiry followed, several company directors had their estates confiscated, and the same year saw a parallel bubble and crash in France around John Law's Mississippi Company.

body.title: Test Yourself
body.question: What made the South Sea Bubble especially dangerous, compared with an ordinary rise in a share price?
options: The company's trade with South America was highly profitable
The company itself lent investors money to buy its shares, using those same shares as collateral
Shares could only be bought with gold coins
The British government guaranteed the share price
body.explanation: When a company finances demand for its own stock, rising prices create more collateral, which supports more lending and more buying. When prices fall, the same loop forces selling. There was no government guarantee, and the South American trade was small.

children.text: Railway Mania: Britain, the 1840s

Railway Mania is the most important of the three for modern investors, because the underlying idea was completely right. Railways did transform Britain's economy, just as the internet later transformed the world's. The problem was price and quantity: far too many lines were proposed, many duplicating each other, funded by investors who assumed every railway would pay dividends like the first successful ones.

body.title: Railway Mania from proof to bust

events.title: Proof of concept
events.description: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opens, the first intercity line to carry passengers on a timetable using steam locomotives. It is profitable, and railway shares gain a reputation as safe dividend payers.

events.title: Cheap money
events.description: Interest rates in Britain are low and government bonds pay little. Investors looking for better income turn to railway shares, which are paying healthy dividends.

events.title: Mania
events.description: Hundreds of new railway companies are promoted. Newspapers devoted to railway shares spring up. Shares can be bought by paying a small deposit, with the rest due later in instalments called calls, so ordinary savers take on large commitments.

events.title: Parliament approves a flood of lines
events.description: Parliament passes 272 Acts authorising new railways, covering roughly 9,500 miles of track. Every one of those companies now needs to call up the rest of its capital from shareholders.

events.title: Calls, rising rates and the bust
events.description: As interest rates rise and companies demand payment on part-paid shares, investors are forced to sell other assets or dump railway shares to raise cash. Share prices fall sharply, and the commercial crisis of 1847 deepens the damage.

events.title: The Railway King falls
events.description: George Hudson, the promoter known as the Railway King, is exposed for practices including paying dividends out of capital rather than profits. He loses his position and reputation.

body.title: The Sting of a Part-Paid Share
body.prompt: In 1845 an investor buys 100 railway shares with a full value of £20 each, paying a deposit of £2 per share, a total of £200. The remaining £18 per share will be called later. By the time the company calls it, fully paid shares trade at only £12. After paying the call, how large is the investor's loss as a percentage of the original £200 deposit?
body.explanation: Total paid = £200 deposit + (100 × £18) call = £2,000. Value of 100 fully paid shares at £12 = £1,200. Loss = £2,000 − £1,200 = £800, which is 400% of the £200 the investor originally put in. The small deposit hid the real commitment. A 40% fall in the share price became a loss four times the initial outlay, exactly the leverage trap from Lesson 1.3.

children.text: There is a direct Indian connection. After the bust, British investors were wary of railway risk. When lines began to be built in India, starting with the Bombay to Thane service in 1853, companies such as the Great Indian Peninsula Railway and the East Indian Railway were promised a guaranteed return of 5% a year on their capital, paid by the colonial government in India if the lines did not earn it. British shareholders got safety. Indian revenues carried the risk.

columns.label: Bubbles that leave little behind
points: Tulip Mania: after the crash, the bulbs were still just bulbs
South Sea Bubble: a financial scheme with a small real business underneath
Value was mostly transferred from late buyers to early sellers
The main legacy is regulation and cautionary tales

columns.label: Bubbles that build something
points: Railway Mania: Britain's rail network roughly doubled in the years that followed
Cheap capital funded infrastructure the economy used for a century
The economy and society won, but many of the investors who paid for it lost
The same pattern returns with the telecom and internet boom of the late 1990s

body.text: "This technology will change the world" and "this stock is a good investment" are two separate claims. Railway investors in 1845 were right about the first and wrong about the second. The question is never just whether the story is true, but what price you are paying for it and how many competitors that price will attract.

children.text: Same Script, Different Costumes

The economic historian Charles Kindleberger, building on Minsky's work, described a sequence that fits almost every mania in his 1978 book Manias, Panics, and Crashes. The table maps our three episodes onto it, with a modern Indian echo alongside.

body.caption: The five stages of a mania

cells: Exotic, hard-to-breed flowers in a newly rich society
Converting national debt into company shares
A proven, profitable new transport technology
Small companies able to list on the NSE Emerge and BSE SME platforms
Contracts traded with little cash down
Instalment buying and company loans against shares
Strong listing-day gains attract new applicants
Share price up about seven times in six months
Tiny issues oversubscribed hundreds of times
Regulators raise concerns about some issuers and tighten rules
Still unfolding. Check how many of these issues trade below their IPO price today

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: In Kindleberger's sequence, the first stage, when a genuine new opportunity catches investors' attention, is called ___.
body.explanation: Displacement is the trigger: a new technology, a policy change or a new market that creates real profit opportunities. Boom, euphoria, distress and revulsion follow.

body.title: Spot the Stage
body.scenario: In August 2024 a small Delhi-based company running two motorcycle dealerships raised about ₹12 crore through an SME IPO, and the issue was subscribed more than 400 times. Around the same period, social media groups were full of screenshots of first-day listing gains, and first-time investors were opening demat accounts specifically to apply for SME IPOs.
body.prompt: Which of Kindleberger's five stages does this most resemble, what are the warning signs, and what question would a cycle-aware investor ask before applying?
body.modelAnswer: This looks like the euphoria stage. The displacement was real: SME platforms genuinely help small businesses raise capital. But the warning signs are classic. Demand of more than 400 times for a ₹12 crore issue from a business with two dealerships shows that applicants were buying the expectation of a quick listing gain, not the business. New investors entering specifically because of recent gains, and social proof in the form of screenshots, both echo the railway promoters' newspapers of 1845. A cycle-aware investor would ask: what would I pay for this business if it could never be sold to someone else at a higher price? What are its revenue, profit and debt? And how many issues from the same period now trade below their IPO price? Those questions are exactly the ones euphoria makes people skip.

cards.definition: Dutch Republic, winter 1636 to 1637. Rare tulip bulbs traded through forward contracts at extreme prices before collapsing in February 1637.
London, 1720. A company swapping government debt for its own shares pushed its price up about seven times, then fell more than 80%, helped by instalment buying and loans against its own shares.
A British law of 1720 banning unchartered joint-stock companies, backed by the South Sea Company to limit rival schemes.
Britain, mid 1840s. Too many railway lines funded with part-paid shares. The network got built, but many investors lost heavily when calls came due and rates rose.
A demand from a company for shareholders to pay the unpaid portion of their shares. Calls turned small deposits into large obligations during Railway Mania.
Displacement, boom, euphoria, distress and revulsion: the typical sequence of a speculative mania.

body.text: India had its own mania in this era. During the American Civil War of 1861 to 1865, cotton prices soared and Bombay was flooded with money, sparking a share frenzy that collapsed when the war ended. Chapter 3 tells that story. Next, Lesson 2.2 moves to the twentieth century, from the Roaring Twenties to the long post-war boom.

Historical prices and figures in this lesson are approximate and drawn from sources that sometimes disagree. The SME IPO example is used only to illustrate a historical pattern and is not a comment on the merits of any specific company or a recommendation to buy or sell any security.

points: Tulip Mania (1636 to 1637) shows how fast prices can detach from value when trading runs on promises rather than cash, though its economic damage has often been exaggerated
The South Sea Company lent investors money to buy its own shares, a pure form of the credit loop, and its price rose about seven times in 1720 before falling more than 80%
Railway Mania proved that a world-changing technology can still be a terrible investment at the wrong price: the network got built, many shareholders were ruined
Part-paid shares were hidden leverage: a £200 deposit could become an £800 loss when calls came due in a falling market
Kindleberger's five stages, displacement, boom, euphoria, distress and revulsion, fit manias from the 1630s to Indian SME IPOs
Before buying into any hot theme, ask what you would pay for the business if you could never sell it to someone else at a higher price
